Wishart measurement model with environmental covariance kernels

Source: R/wishart_covariates.R
wishart_covariates.Rd

Creates a Wishart measurement model whose fitted covariance includes the resistance-implied covariance plus one or more positive semidefinite kernels built from site-level environmental covariates. Use this as the Wishart analogue of mlpe_covariates when your measurement model is generalized_wishart (squared-distance responses) or wishart_covariance (covariance-matrix responses).

Usage

wishart_covariates(
  x,
  coords = NULL,
  transform = c("absdiff", "sqdiff", "euclidean", "manhattan"),
  scale = FALSE,
  model = c("wishart_covariance", "generalized_wishart")
)

Arguments

x

Site-level covariates. Supported inputs are the same as pairwise_endpoint_covariates: a numeric vector, matrix, data frame, or terra::SpatRaster. A previously constructed terradish_pairwise_covariates object is accepted unchanged.

coords

Required when x is a raster. Focal-point coordinates in the same projection as x; accepts the same inputs as conductance_surface.

transform

Pairwise environmental difference: "absdiff" (default), "sqdiff", "euclidean", or "manhattan". See pairwise_endpoint_covariates. Ignored for an existing pairwise-covariate object.

scale

Logical. Standardize site-level covariates to zero mean and unit variance before constructing kernels? Recommended when covariates use different units or scales.

model

Which Wishart likelihood to use. "generalized_wishart" is appropriate only when S is an admissible squared-distance matrix coherently related to a centered positive-semidefinite covariance matrix. An arbitrary distance matrix, including an unchecked \(F_{ST}\) matrix, is not sufficient. "wishart_covariance" is appropriate when S is a covariance matrix (e.g. from cov_from_genetic_data). In both cases the same \(\Sigma\) parameterization is used; they differ in how \(\Sigma\) is compared to the observed data.

Value

A function of class "terradish_measurement_model" suitable for the measurement_model argument of terradish and terradish_grid. The nuisance parameter vector \(\phi\) estimated by terradish contains tau, one lambda_<covariate> per environmental kernel, and sigma (in that order). The function stores the kernel array in attribute "kernel_covariates" and supports site-subsetting for model fitting through terradish.

Details

A zero kernel coefficient sets the boundary flag while retaining conductance inference when the resistance coefficient is positive. Summaries mark zero kernel coefficients and give one-sided upper limits instead of symmetric intervals. Tests adding only kernel coefficients use a chi-bar-square reference with binomial weights. This reference is exact for information-orthogonal kernels and approximate otherwise. MLPE environmental coefficients are unconstrained and retain ordinary chi-square tests.

wishart_covariates() is the Wishart analogue of mlpe_covariates, but environmental covariates enter the model through positive semidefinite kernels. For each pairwise difference matrix \(D_k\), the kernel is \(K_k=-\frac12 H D_k H\), where \(H\) centers sites. A kernel with a negative eigenvalue beyond numerical tolerance is rejected. The "sqdiff" transform gives the centered outer product of the original covariate. The fitted covariance is:

$$\Sigma = \tau E(\theta) + \sum_k \lambda_k K_k + \exp(\sigma) I$$

where \(E(\theta)\) is the resistance-implied covariance (generalized inverse of the graph Laplacian at conductance parameters \(\theta\)), \(\tau\) is the weight on conductance-implied covariance, \(\lambda_k \geq 0\) are nonnegative kernel weights, and \(\exp(\sigma)\) is diagonal residual variance not represented by the graph or environmental kernels.

The nuisance parameters estimated alongside \(\theta\) are:

tau

Nonnegative scale on the resistance-implied covariance \(E\). A value near zero indicates no detectable contribution from conductance-implied covariance under this model.

lambda_<covariate>

Nonnegative weight per unit of the corresponding pairwise environmental difference. A negative association is represented at the zero bound; MLPE environmental slopes are unconstrained. The weight is not a causal IBE effect.

sigma

Log-scale nugget: identity component added as \(\exp(\sigma) I\), representing diagonal variance not captured by the other covariance components. It is not a smoothing scale or direct drift or population-size estimate.

This design naturally preserves positive definiteness of \(\Sigma\) when the nugget is positive and all kernel weights are nonnegative. It is evaluated on site contrasts, as in wishart_covariance. The implied squared-distance mean is \(\tau R_{ij}+\sum_k\lambda_k D_{k,ij} +2\exp(\sigma)\), using the same additive environmental terms as MLPE. The likelihoods and coefficient constraints still differ. Use wishart_covariates() when the response satisfies the selected Wishart model's requirements and you can justify an effective degrees-of-freedom value nu; use mlpe_covariates when nu is unknown or when the distance-regression framework better matches the response. Neither formulation cleanly separates causal IBE from IBR when predictors and kernels are spatially correlated. Scaling is applied to site values before the pairwise transform; kernels are not normalized afterward. Site subsets retain these original pairwise values and rebuild centered kernels without restandardizing the subset. In an unpublished development null simulation, AIC selected an environmental kernel in 19 of 40 runs at the SNP-count value of nu, and in none at a replicate-calibrated value. These are results of that design, not general error-rate guarantees. Use terradish_rescale_nu for sensitivity and terradish_cv_folds(..., nuisance = "fixed") to assess predictive support for a measurement-model extension.

Numerical nugget limits

Fitting uses the same small-nugget safeguards as wishart_covariance, retaining supplied bounds and fixed parameters. A verified numerical zero residual-variance limit does not remove the graph or environmental kernel coefficients. summary() omits Wald uncertainty for the log-scale nugget at that limit.

Worked example

See vignette("v08-ibe-ibr-workflow", package = "terradish") for environmental covariance kernels and their distinction from MLPE slopes.

Interpreting pairwise effects

Construct one pairwise_covariates object to use the same environmental transforms and geographic distances in both likelihood families. Their fitted conductance surfaces are conditional on these terms, and conductance signs can change when the mean structure changes. Report fits with and without pairwise effects. A uniform ~ 1 conductance model with pairwise terms represents IBD plus IBE, not IBE alone.

A positive environmental coefficient means differentiation increases with environmental difference conditional on resistance. It does not distinguish assortative mating, dispersal filtering, local adaptation, or site variance that rises at environmental extremes. MLPE coefficients are unconstrained; Wishart kernel weights are nonnegative. Compare their effects in resistance-distance units with terradish_ibe_ratio, which divides by the resistance coefficient and propagates joint uncertainty. Ratios are undefined when that denominator is zero.

Effective Wishart information

For Wishart likelihoods, nu scales the log likelihood. Point estimates do not depend on it, but standard errors, likelihood-ratio tests, and information criteria do. It is a dispersion parameter that you set, rather than the number of markers. Linkage and the population history shared by loci can make effective information much smaller than the SNP count. In unpublished forward-time simulations run during development, standard errors at the SNP count were three to five times smaller than the spread among replicate histories. Those model-based errors understated uncertainty.

Use terradish_cv_folds to compare conductance formulas, and terradish_rescale_nu to report inference across plausible values. For the same successful folds and nuisance settings, changing nu rescales Wishart CV scores without changing their ranking. Neither procedure identifies the true effective information or repairs an unsuitable response matrix.

References

McCullagh P. 2009. Marginal likelihood for distance matrices. Statistica Sinica 19:631-649.

Examples

library(terra)

data(melip)
covariates <- c(terra::unwrap(melip.altitude),
                terra::unwrap(melip.forestcover))
coords <- terra::unwrap(melip.coords)
names(covariates) <- c("altitude", "forestcover")
# Coarsened so the example runs quickly; name layers, then scale.
covariates <- scale_covariates(terra::aggregate(covariates, fact = 3,
                                                na.rm = TRUE))
# Keep one site per raster cell (some melip sites share a cell).
keep <- !duplicated(terra::cellFromXY(covariates, terra::crds(coords)))
coords <- coords[keep]
Fst <- melip.Fst[keep, keep]
surface <- conductance_surface(covariates, coords)

# Build an altitude kernel for a covariance-Wishart model.
g_wc <- wishart_covariates(terra::unwrap(melip.altitude), coords = coords,
                           model = "wishart_covariance", scale = TRUE)
inherits(g_wc, "terradish_measurement_model")  # TRUE
#> [1] TRUE

# Simulate an admissible covariance response, then fit the extended model.
# The simulator takes the nugget variance on its natural scale (0.2); the
# fitted `sigma` is its logarithm.
# \donttest{
simulated <- simulate_covariance_response(
  theta = c(altitude = 0.2, forestcover = -0.1),
  formula = ~ altitude + forestcover,
  data = surface, tau = 0.8, sigma = 0.2, nu = 40, seed = 1
)
fit_joint_w <- terradish(
  simulated$covariance ~ altitude + forestcover,
  data              = surface,
  conductance_model = loglinear_conductance,
  measurement_model = g_wc,
  nu                = 40
)
# phi table shows tau, lambda_altitude, and sigma (log nugget).
summary(fit_joint_w)
#> Conductance surface with 2531 vertices (31 focal) estimated by maximum likelihood
